newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan coffee auctions to resume this week.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan coffee auctions to resume this week.

text.p: Kenya's weekly coffee export auctions are likely to resume on Tuesday after a postponement from last week, coffee traders said on Monday.
They said last week the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) created an acute market shortage after it had sold more stocks than usual in preceding weeks to meet payment obligations to farmers.
Last week's auction was postponed on tight supply.
Auction officials said the coffee board had not accumulated enough coffee to sell last Tuesday and this week.
On Monday, board officials said auctions would resume on Tuesday.
Traders said the coffee board had created the current shortage by pushing a lot of coffee into the market, so as to meet payment obligations to coffee farmers.
"Farmers have been pushing for money, and the board did not want to be blamed for non-payment," one trader said.

Another trader said that with the liberalisation of the coffee market, farmers had been pressurising them to auction immediately. But they could not meet the weekly demand due to delayed delivery by some small-scale farmers.
"The delivery is very slow. In fact, some of this season's crop that was harvested in September, is still undergoing the milling process," the trader added.
Another trader said the prices had been so low that some farmers had withheld their stock.
The coffee auction normally averages 17,000 bags a week during the minor crop season, which lasts for about the last six months of the year, according to leading coffee houses.

After the Tuesday sales, the auction will be on recess until January. Traders said they expected good demand for grades AA, AB and PB to continue, although they predicted availability would go down by 10 percent.

They said coffee procurement from farmers in the smallholder cooperative sector had declined because they could not afford the high cost of fumigating their coffee crop against the coffee berry disease and had instead resorted to intercropping to cover their earnings.
